questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: As I had already learned German for an exchange that were cancelled due to COVID, it was crucial that it was in Germany. Besides that, the most crucial aspect was the academic opportunities - I wanted to explore a different academic culture with another approach on a high level. Other important aspects was that it was a beautiful city and close to nature.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was such an amazing experience! I have learned so much, I really gained inside into the culture of Heidelberg and got to know many locals and I made some really nice friends and also had a bit of time for travelling. I am VERY happy, that I took this opportunity, and it has definitely been a formative experience for me. When it doesn't score a perfect 10, it is because the workload at the university could be quite overwhelming and because it was sometimes quite a struggle to find my way through German bureaucracy.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: This was surely one of the most challenging aspects of the exchange. Everyone was very helpful, but the whole process is spread across many institutions, so it can be quite difficult to know who to ask for help - the history department in DK, the international department there, the history department in Heidelberg, the international department there, the city municipality in Heidelberg, the Studierendenwerk etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, people at all the abovementioned institutions were very helpful. When I came with questions they helped answering them, but I wasn't always sure what to ask were. I came a month before my exhange began for a language course, which meant that the introductory meetings that were given came at a time when I no longer needed the information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was lucky and got a room through "Studierendenwerk", so for me it was quite automatic. But as a student city, there is a lack of housing in Heidelberg, meaning that it can be quite challenging to find housing. If you don't succeed in finding housing through Studierendenwerk, there are WG-Gesucht and/or a few Facebook Groups.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
If you get housing through Studierendenwerk, it is incredibly cheap - between 200 and 300 euro. But is a gamble, as you don't know if you would get housing in the outskirts or right by the university. Additionally, men can get in housing in "Studentenverbindungen" - they are old traditional frat houses, which are amazing old houses very cheap in central locations. Some of them are fine, but other have some problematic affiliations and can be very right-leaning. Just something to be aware of:
https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/bildung/heidelberg-mutmasslich-antisemitische-attacke-burschenschaft-distanziert-sich-a-0cd9be76-7c7f-48f3-8d17-5162ad0182de

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Most of my friends living by Studierendenwerk were very pleased with the housing, especially if you can get a place in one the "Europa-Häuser", those are amazing places to live. But I lived in the outskirts in a place that wasn't very nice. Once you moved in, it can be hard to get out of the contract before the end of the exchange. So even though I tried for many months and also had quite a lot of problems with my roomies, it was not possible to change and not a lot of help was given. So I was not so satisfied, but it is really a matter of luck, and most people are super happy about the housing.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a little messy, but it worked out fine in the end.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I registered from home during the summer. Then I went there in the end of August, but as the semester didn't start until 1st of October, it took some time, before I could register. I honestly cannot remember the whole process, but there were some meetings to guide us through the process, and then you fill out a few papers and give to a few persons. You also pay a fee of around 200 Euros for the semester.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above, there were a few meetings. You could come to both History Department and International Department with questions, but you didn't always know what to ask or where to go.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very! I had a lot of really great courses and I got everything I wanted. But you have to write the professor or assistant to register (google "Kommentiertes Vorlesungsverzeichnis Heidelberg Geschichte" to see the courses and who to write), and a few courses were already full at that point.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you want to be sure to get the courses you want, look for subjects in good time. The course catalogue is usually published 2/3 months before the start of the semester, and you can register even before you enroll. Just write the professor of the course, most of them are super nice
AND I had a prejudice about Germany being super strict and always following the rules very thoroughly. But the process of registering for courses was a lot more relaxed than in Denmark. In the start, I was panicking about deadlines coming up and still not receiving a lot of information on courses. But then I discovered, that I just needed to be more patient, as everything worked out in the end. People also register for more classes than they need and go to all in the first week to hear more, after that they decide. There is a second registration for exams later in the semester, and that is really the binding registration.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I learned so much and have really grown academically! There were a lot of courses to choose from, and they were all great. I would recommend, though, that you try to learn German beforehand. I was in no way fluent as I got there, and I didn't get a lot the first month. But as a Dane, it is possible to pick up the language, if you have some forehand knowledge. You don't have nearly as many courses to choose from, if you can only speak English. AND the workload is a lot bigger than in Denmark. Most students here don't have holidays during the five years of university, because there are so many subjects to be completed. So accept that you can't do perfect in all subjects.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Many people study their BA in Heidelberg and then go elsewhere (typically Berlin) for the MA. This means, that there is a somewhat limited number of MA-Students in Heidelberg, and classes often combine BA- and MA-studentes. Perhaps because of my difficulties with the language of teaching, I still found it quite challenging, it is a really high level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: You have a lot of different formats in comparison to Denmark. The Vorlesungen are like the Danish Forelæsninger with a teacher talking and students asking questions in the end. But e.g. Übungen and Kolloquien are mainly student-driven. In general, the teaching is more driven by students than in Denmark. It is harder to get by, if you haven't read beforehand, and students are asked to think somewhat more freely than in Denmark, I found (somewhat surprisingly) - for example, in several subjects I had to develop my own research design in a degree of freedom, that I only know from my BA-thesis in Denmark. You also work with more personal academic genres, like essays (a la Susan Sontag) and Blogs.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Kunst und Kultur in der Krise in den „roaring twenties“ - 2 ECTS
- Körper(um)welten (Marsiliusbrückenseminar)
- „Alleinstehende Frauen“, „Freundinnen“, „Frauenliebende Frauen“ - Lesbische
Lebenswelten im deutschen Südwesten (ca. 1920er-1960er Jahre)
- Geschichtsphilosophie
- „Auf der Suche nach der verlorenen Wahrheit.“ Begriff und Problem der Wahrheit in
 der Geschichtswissenschaft zwischen Historismus und Gegenwart
- Multisensory Histories: Archives and Methods in South Asian Studies
- Violence and Non-Violence in Colonial India

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you have the possiblity, take part in a Marsilius-Brücken Seminar!! They are interdisciplinary seminars, where you develop a project on your own and then discuss it. I had one on the relationship between bodies and environments between history, ethnography, literary studies and biologies - and it was definitely one of the most interesting courses I ever had.
There is a lot to choose from, but I was especially happy for Kama Maclean and Karen Nolte. Both where very helpful, when I didn't get things as a foreigner, and they both have an innovating and exciting approach to teaching and research.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The prices for internet and telephone. It is quite a lot more expensive than in Denmark and most often you are obliged to pay for at least two years, so that was really unhandy. I got someone to take over my internet as I left and I bought "taletid" at ALDI (ALDI TALK), because it is without binding. But I lost the SIM-card and got lazy, so I just used my Danish phone, even though my free roaming went away after two months and it got crazy expensive. Food, personal spending and transport can be done quite a lot cheaper, I lived the good life.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Alcohol and candy are cheap, so that's nice. Housing was a lot cheaper than expected and food in the Cantina/Mensa is also quite cheap. I was surprised of the prices for phone and internet.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have a lot, but as it was the pandemic, I did not participate in a lot.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: BUDDY-program, where you get set up with a fulltime student from your subject, who can show you around and often make friends with. ENS (Erasmus Student Network) arranges A LOT of events for exchange students, which I used a lot in the start to make friends. They have a lot of high school sports, a choir, a student council, a philharmonic orchestra etc. I was not involved in this, but if there hadn't been a pandemic, they had a lot of fun alternative sports really cheap.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Two institutions were decisive for my stay in Heidelberg. 
One is Clemens in the bookstore "Artes Liberales" - he is really friendly, has an amazing knowledge of literature and does a lot for the local community. He has the bookstore as well as "Universitas", another room which you can loan, where he makes weekly readings and a lot of other events. He even agreed to make a reading group for me and a few friends - every second week he would bring wine and teach us about great literature and the German language for free! 
His "Stammkneipe" is called Orange, and it is the most wonderful place I have ever been to. The owners Claudia and Osama are incredibly friendly. As I didn't feel so well at my home in Heidelberg, this bar really became a second home to me. I made a lot of friends there from actors and musicians at the Heidelberger Theater to the old secretary of Gadamer, who also studied by Koselleck. Through this bar I really got integrated in the local intellectual environment, in a way I did not think possible.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try to spend as much time as possible in Orange. Apart from that take advantage of the fact, that you are living in the middle of Europe - it is so easy and cheap to get to Alsace and Strassbourg, to Frankfurt, to Freiburg and Schwarzwald or to Basel. So travel as much as you can, I discovered this a tad late, but still had some nice travels in Germany, France and Italy. Also discover the Odenwald and go hike in the mountains as often as possible, as they will be right by your doorstep.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: There was a language barrier to overcome, but after that I found it surprisingly easy - I do not think there are really large cultural differences between Germany and Denmark

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: ORANGE!!! And try picking courses in German, I was often the only non-German in class, which meant that people took an interest in me and were really friendly. "Local" is also not a very meaningful thing in Heidelberg, as most students come from other cities to study in Heidelberg. I only met one person born in Heidelberg during my stay. As the city is 25 % students, this means that most people are really eager to get to know others, as everyone is in the same boat.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Language and academic culture. People were patient and helpful, but the course formats are quite different, as are the exams.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: As an old university city, it is quite snobbish. This can be quite disgusting, as when people in Heidelberg critique the neighboring Mannheim for being more working class. But it also means, that there is a great interest in history, literature and philosophy, which you can discuss with most people. Also the Theater is free for students, meaning you have access to endless plays, concerts and dance performances. I really appreciated the opennes, people were in general a lot more friendly than expected and really made me feel at home.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Learn German. I was in no way fluent as I arrived, and had to struggle with this for the first few months. But by learning German I had access to a lot more interesting courses as well as making friends with German students and other inhabitants in the city. I think my stay would have been quite different, if I didn't know German.
2. Balance your study - I was quite bad at this and got really stressed at times, because of the huge workload. So accept that you are going to perform mediocre and then just delve into the things you find the most interesting.
3. Travel a lot! I discovered this too late, but in the end I went somewhere every weekend. You can easily go somewhere like Karlsruhe or Bad Wimpfen to just spend the day there, and with one night in a hostel, you also have time to see Freiburg or Strassbourg.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Yes, go to Orange as often as you can :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My academic gain! I really learned a lot here and feel like I grew from a student just attending classes to someone who has a clear understanding of the direction in which I want to research.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably the German bureaucracy. All the different phone numbers, things that cannot be done online, the running to letterboxes and being passed on to the next office. I understand why Kafka wrote "The Trial" in German. And Weber even developed his theory of Bureaucracy in Heidelberg, which makes sense to me :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go there, have fun, stay in school!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
